title: How to Use Microsoft Clarity to Increase Shopify Conversion Rate
meta_title: Microsoft Clarity for Shopify: Raise Conversion Rate
meta_description: How we use Microsoft Clarity on Shopify stores: heatmaps first, click maps, smart events, conversion maps and a 5-step method for session recordings.
teaser: The exact order we use Microsoft Clarity in, from heatmaps to recordings, that took one store from 1% to 2.1% conversion rate.
summary: Microsoft Clarity shows why Shopify visitors drop off, while GA4 only shows where. Start with heatmaps and click maps across thousands of sessions, use smart events and conversion maps to see which elements relate to purchases, then watch filtered session recordings to find patterns you turn into A/B test hypotheses. On one store, this process took the conversion rate from 1% to 2.1% in 90 days.
key_takeaways: Look at heatmaps before session recordings: heatmaps combine thousands of users at once, recordings show one at a time.
Change Clarity's default 3-day date range to around the last 30 days, or to whatever period matches how often your site changes.
Check your collection page scroll and click maps. If visitors only see the first two rows, put your bestsellers there and label them as bestsellers.
Use the product page click map to see which accordions, size guides or gallery images get the most clicks, then surface that information near the add to cart button.
Use conversion maps to compare the conversion rate of users who clicked an element (like a size guide accordion) with those who did not, so you know which elements earn their place.
Filter by referrer and by browser, OS and device: cold ad traffic, organic traffic, mobile and desktop users behave very differently.
Watch recordings only after finding the drop-off in GA4 or Shopify, filtered to sessions over 15 seconds, sorted by most clicks, at 2x or 4x speed, and look for patterns across 15 to 20 of them.

sections.heading: Why use Microsoft Clarity if you already have GA4?

blocks.text: Improving your conversion rate is not that difficult once you know what to improve. The problem is that **GA4 tells you where the problem is, not why**. It shows you which page loses people, but it can't show you what those people were trying to do.

Microsoft Clarity fills that gap. It shows exactly how users interact with your store, so you understand what needs to change. On one store we worked on, we used Clarity heatmaps to come up with a list of test hypotheses within 20 minutes. After 90 days of testing, the conversion rate went from **1% to 2.1%**.
Below is the exact order we use Clarity in, and how you can apply it to your own Shopify store.

sections.heading: Should you start with heatmaps or session recordings?

blocks.text: Start with heatmaps. Recordings are fun to watch, but you can only watch one at a time. They take time, they're tedious, and if you're looking at the wrong data you can watch tons of them and learn nothing.

Heatmaps combine thousands, even hundreds of thousands of users at once. They tell you which page or section deserves your attention. Once you know what you want to understand, then you go into the recordings.

items: **Change the date range.** Clarity defaults to the last 3 days. Set it to something like the last 30 days, or adjust it to how often your site changes, so the data is relevant.

**Fix blocked screenshots.** If a newsletter pop-up or cookie banner covers the heatmap, Clarity isn't broken: the screenshot it captured includes the pop-up. Use the option to change the screenshot and pick a different render of the page.

sections.heading: How do you spot buried bestsellers on a collection page?

blocks.text: The first thing I look at is what I call the **buried bestseller problem**. A visitor lands on a collection page and only sees the first two rows of products. The scroll heatmap shows people don't scroll that far, and the click map shows they click very high on the page.

That's only a problem if your products are ordered badly. Your bestsellers usually have better reviews and better product quality, so they should be at the top. Calling them "bestseller" also gives the user more confidence.

Say you have 24 or 25 products and the customer only sees 30% of the page. That's six or seven products. If those aren't your best ones, you're losing clicks. **Order your products so the strongest ones are seen first**, and you'll get a better click-through rate and a higher conversion rate.

sections.heading: What does the product page click map tell you about customer anxiety?

blocks.text: On the product page, I use the click map to find out what customers are anxious about. GA4 could track clicks too, but tracking every element on a page is tedious. **Clarity tracks every click by default.**

Visitors scroll the page with a limited view, especially on mobile, and they click where they want more information: the gallery, the variant selector, the size guide, or accordions about shipping details below the fold. Where their clicks cluster is the question they most want answered.

items: If an accordion gets a lot of clicks, people want information that's hidden. Many more want it but never click. Surface it, for example by adding shipping details around the add to cart button.
If the size guide gets a lot of attention, answer the question upfront, for example by stating that the model is 5'4" and wears size S.

blocks.text: Then look at **dead click clusters**. Customers click because they expect something to happen, but there's no link or functionality. Often they click again, and some turn into rage clicks. Those clusters show you where people wish there was something, so you can make that functionality real.

sections.heading: How do smart events work in Microsoft Clarity?

blocks.text: Clarity automatically captures events known from Shopify, like add to cart, seeing reviews and making a purchase. You can **filter heatmaps and recordings by the event a user triggered**.

For example, filter on the see reviews event and compare those users with the ones who didn't see a review. Maybe they were more confident. Maybe they jumped straight to the reviews instead of scrolling top to bottom. That tells you what to surface more or make easier to find.

Say there's one particular review on a bestselling product that everybody wants to see. Some might leave, but maybe most who saw it did buy. Filtering by events shows you what those users do differently from everyone else.

sections.heading: What is a conversion map in Microsoft Clarity?

blocks.text: This is the feature nobody talks about and we use all the time. A conversion map adds ecommerce data to the heatmaps tab, so you see what people clicked on or saw together with the purchase data tied to it.

Take a product page with accordions for shipping details, return policy and size guide. Say 100 people clicked the size guide. Click the element and you can see how many of those users made a purchase. If their conversion rate is double that of people who didn't click it, you know that element matters.
You can actually really understand how an element on your site contributes to the performance without even having to A/B test it.

You can do this per element for conversion rate, revenue or sessions, including reviews and collection page changes. It's especially useful for new elements. If nobody clicks a new accordion, it added no value. If people click it but convert at a lower rate than those who don't, they probably aren't getting anything from it, so **remove it or A/B test it**.

sections.heading: Why filter Clarity by referrer, browser and device?

blocks.text: Users from **cold ads** and users from **organic search** behave very differently. Organic visitors had the intent to come to your site, so they read more, look at all the images and probably convert at a higher rate. Cold traffic just clicked an ad and spends less time learning about the product.

For cold traffic, make things easy to understand, readily available and a bit quicker. Returning customers and organic visitors take their time, so longer copy that educates can work. Combine the referrer filter with conversion maps to see which elements contribute more for each group. At some point you can use that to personalise the experience for cold and warm segments.

Then filter by **browser, operating system and device**. You see your site through your own screen, which is very different from a smaller, bigger or different screen. Desktop and mobile differ in user experience and performance. Don't just design mobile first: verify that everything works for customers on every device. You'll often find bugs this way.

sections.heading: How do you watch session recordings without wasting hours?

blocks.text: Recordings are an important tool, but watching random ones won't give you any answers. This is the five-step process we use:

items: Find where customers leave the funnel. Use GA4 or Shopify to see whether the biggest drop is on the product page, cart or checkout.
In Clarity, filter by that page. Only include sessions longer than 15 seconds and users relevant to your question, otherwise you're watching people who never intended to buy.
Sort the list from most clicks to fewest. This filters out users who weren't engaged.
Watch at 2x or 4x speed. Skipping inactivity is possible but often gives a strange view.
Watch 15 to 20 recordings and look for what's common across them.

blocks.text: The tricky part is interpretation. Someone might rage click an element a million times and still buy. **One frustrating moment in one recording doesn't mean changing that element will move conversion rate.** Look for patterns: where people often scroll to, what information they're searching for, and how you can surface it better.

sections.heading: The full loop: GA4, Clarity, hypothesis, A/B test

items: Use GA4 or Shopify to find where users abandon the most. That's the biggest problem to solve.
Open Clarity to understand why: how those users behave, what they look for, what they miss and where they click.
Turn those observations into hypotheses: changes you believe will improve performance.
A/B test them to see if the change actually makes or breaks the bank.
After the test, compare how users engaged with the winning and losing variants in Clarity.

blocks.text: That last step is often forgotten. Comparing behaviour across variants tells you whether the element really drove the improvement, or whether there's still more you can do. We've run this process hundreds of times, and it's how we approach every new brand we work with.

faq.q: What is the difference between GA4 and Microsoft Clarity?
faq.a: GA4 tells you where visitors drop off in your funnel, but not why. Microsoft Clarity shows how users actually interact with your store through heatmaps, click maps and session recordings, so you can understand the reason behind the drop-off.

faq.q: Should I look at heatmaps or session recordings first in Clarity?
faq.a: Heatmaps first. They combine thousands of users at once and show you which page or section needs attention. Recordings show one user at a time and are slow to watch, so only go into them once you know what question you're trying to answer.

faq.q: What date range should I use in Microsoft Clarity?
faq.a: Clarity defaults to the last 3 days, which is usually too short. Change it to something like the last 30 days, or match it to how often your site changes so the data reflects the current version of your store.

faq.q: What is a conversion map in Microsoft Clarity?
faq.a: A conversion map adds ecommerce data to the heatmaps tab. You can click an element, such as a size guide accordion, and see the conversion rate, revenue or sessions of users who engaged with it. If those users convert at double the rate of others, the element is important; if they convert lower or nobody clicks, consider removing or A/B testing it.

faq.q: How many Clarity session recordings should I watch?
faq.a: Watch 15 to 20 recordings per question. Filter first to the page with the highest drop-off, to sessions longer than 15 seconds, sort by most clicks, and watch at 2x or 4x speed. Look for patterns across recordings rather than reacting to one user's behaviour.

faq.q: What are dead clicks and rage clicks in Clarity?
faq.a: Dead clicks are clicks on something that doesn't respond because there's no link or functionality. When users keep clicking repeatedly, those become rage clicks. Clusters of them show where customers expect something to happen, so you can add that functionality.
